newsitem.title: USA: U.S. unions show new vitality, but not membership.
newsitem.headline: U.S. unions show new vitality, but not membership.

text.p: The once-moribund U.S. labour movement is showing signs of a resurgence of spunk and vitality -- but not higher membership yet.

With heightened political activism, high-profile organising drives and innovative tactics, the nation's largest labour federation, the AFL-CIO, has infused staff members and its 78 affiliated unions with new energy under its president, John Sweeney, labour scholars said in recent interviews.
"They are doing the things that seem to be a prerequisite for a revival of the union movement," said labour historian Nelson Lichtenstein of the University of Virginia.

If the labour movement is to rebuild itself, it will not do so in small increments, but rather in some dramatic episode that builds on groundwork now being laid, he said. Until then, however, the 40-year downtrend in membership continues.

Last year, union membership fell to 16.3 million, only 14.5 percent of wage and salaried employees, from 16.4 million, or 14.9 percent, in 1995. Membership peaked in the 1950s when about one-third of all workers carried union cards.

The U.S. work force ranks among the lowest in unionization of industrialised countries. Union membership rates are above 50 percent of workers in Australia and Ireland, 24.1 percent in Japan, 29.2 percent in Canada and 35.5 percent in Germany. In Britain, 40 percent of workers are covered by union contracts.
In the U.S. private sector, union representation is even thinner, covering only 10.2 percent of employees.

Labour scholars say Sweeney has sought to restore a culture of organising to the labour movement since he was elected in October 1995 with a promise to make unions relevant again. This year, the AFL-CIO dedicated one-third of its $90 million budget to organising. More importantly, many of its affiliated unions are investing more money and effort on organising.
"They understand that right now they are losing several hundred thousand members a year," said Lichtenstein. "They understand that this is a big problem and it cannot be solved in routine fashion."

One new approach has been the "Union Cities" programme. In its showcase city of Las Vegas, the AFL-CIO is coordinating organising drives by its unions with the goal of signing up most, if not all, workers in key industries like construction, hotels and restaurants. Other cities are being added.

"That type of approach, where there's an effort to organise all the workers in one market, really makes a lot of sense," said Rick Hurd, director of labour studies at Cornell University's School of Industrial and Labour Relations.
Elsewhere, organising efforts are accelerating, especially those aimed at low-wage workers in health care and other service occupations that cannot easily be exported.

Unions with a history of aggressive organising have stepped up their drives in the poultry and textile industries in the union-hostile South. In a well publicised effort, the AFL-CIO is helping the United Farm Workers in its national campaign to represent 20,000 California strawberry workers.

To bring new blood to the labour movement, the AFL-CIO is now in its second annual "Union Summer" programme, reminiscent of 1960s civil rights era voter registration drives, in which 500 young people spend vacations working on organising campaigns.
With a low unemployment rate reducing the fear of job loss, scholars said there may never be a better time for unions to recruit members. It may be now or never.

"If union membership is not going up as a share of the work force in the private sector by the end of the century, then the labour movement is in serious trouble," said Hurd. "Employers are watching now to see if the new tactics are working."

Even though many strikes ended in disaster for unions since 1980 as employers quickly hired permanent replacements, some unions have shown that the strike weapon is still viable, especially against companies that have made themselves vulnerable by operating with "just-in-time" inventories.

At General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp., strikes at selected plants by the United Auto Workers, mostly over job security and excessive overtime, cut nearly $1 billion from net earnings of the two carmakers in the second quarter.
"It seems to me that maybe they're taking a little bit more aggressive stance at the bargaining table," said industrial relations Professor Raymond Hilgert of Washington University in St. Louis.

Strike activity is still near historically low levels. There were only 37 major work stoppages last year, up from an all-time low of 31 in 1995 and compared with more than 1,000 or 2,000 a year in most years before 1980.

On the political front, the AFL-CIO is following up last year's $35 million media blitz against congressional Republicans with several more rounds of issue-oriented attack ads against lawmakers, including some Democrats.

Borrowing from the strategy of the conservative Christian Coalition, the AFL-CIO has sought to leverage the power of its unions' 13.1 million members into even greater political clout with its carefully targeted advertising campaigns.
While the plan to oust the House Republican majority fell short, labour has stopped much legislation it opposes.
Scholars say Sweeney's tactics will have to produce a membership turnaround within two or three years -- around the end of his second term, assuming he is re-elected in October.
"He's raised a lot of expectations," said Hilgert. "By the end of the second term, that's when they'll probably say, 'OK, you've had your chance, John.'"
